At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3701)

Disaggregated serving separates prefill and decode onto distinct worker pools, which means prefill latency variance — not just mean prefill time — directly determines how often decode workers stall waiting for KV cache transfers, and under heterogeneous prompt length distributions this variance is structurally amplified: short prompts finish prefill quickly and flood the KV transfer bus while long prompts hold prefill workers for hundreds of milliseconds, creating a bimodal occupancy pattern that neither a FIFO nor a shortest-job-first scheduler handles gracefully. Chunked attention scheduling — breaking long prompts into fixed-size chunks processed across multiple prefill steps — was introduced precisely to bound per-step latency, but it introduces a subtler problem: a prompt split across k chunks occupies a prefill worker slot across k scheduling epochs, so the effective head-of-line blocking isn't eliminated, it's temporally smeared, and under bursty arrival the smearing creates correlated stalls across the decode fleet. The central question is therefore not "what is average prefill time?" but rather "what is the covariance structure of prefill completion times across concurrent requests, and how does that covariance propagate into decode-side KV cache availability jitter?" An expert worries about something a beginner entirely misses: chunk boundary alignment interacts with attention sparsity patterns, so prompts with dense cross-token dependencies (e.g., long-range coreference in retrieval-augmented contexts) pay a disproportionate KV recomputation penalty at chunk seams if prefix caching granularity doesn't align with chunk boundaries, making latency variance a function of prompt content, not just prompt length. The second-order concern is that dynamic scheduling algorithms that react to queue depth are themselves destabilizing under high variance: they tend to reorder requests in ways that maximize short-term throughput but produce synchronized long-prompt batches that saturate prefill memory bandwidth simultaneously, triggering a variance spike that cascades into a decode stall wave.

When a prefill epoch mixes short-prompt completions with in-flight chunks of long prompts, the KV cache entries for completed short prompts are immediately transferable to decode workers, but they share the same PCIe or RoCE fabric with partial KV writes for the long-prompt chunks still in progress — and because the transfer bus operates on contiguous KV block granularity (typically 128–256 token blocks in systems like vLLM's PagedAttention), a partial chunk that doesn't fill a complete block cannot be flushed until the block is sealed, creating a write-ordering inversion where short-prompt KV data sits in a transfer queue behind an incomplete block fence belonging to the long prompt. DistServe (Zhong et al., 2024) documented this concretely: their disaggregated prototype observed that KV migration latency under mixed-length batches was not bounded by network bandwidth but by block-seal latency, which scaled with the remaining token count in the current chunk of the longest co-scheduled prompt — a dependency invisible to bandwidth-based capacity planning. The hazard is that static chunk-size tuning implicitly assumes all co-scheduled requests are either all chunked or all complete at epoch boundaries, but heterogeneous distributions violate this assumption structurally: a chunk size of 512 tokens chosen to bound prefill latency at p99 for a uniform distribution will, under a heavy-tailed length distribution, frequently produce epochs where one 4096-token prompt contributes 8 sequential chunk boundaries while eight 256-token prompts complete and pile up sealed-but-untransferable KV blocks waiting for the bus to clear. Sarathi-Serve (Agrawal et al., 2024) attempted to address this with stall-free chunked prefill, scheduling chunk sizes dynamically to keep decode batches continuous, but their evaluation showed that under Poisson arrivals with coefficient of variation greater than 1.5 in prompt length, the scheduler's chunk-size decisions based on queue-depth heuristics lagged actual contention by one to two epochs, producing periodic transfer bus saturation spikes. The fundamental reason static tuning cannot resolve this is that the hazard is conditional on the joint arrival state — specifically on how many long prompts happen to be mid-chunk simultaneously — which is a random variable whose distribution shifts with load, time-of-day request mix, and upstream retrieval latency, none of which a fixed chunk-size parameter can track.

During KV transfer bus saturation, prefill workers enter a state that looks deceptively healthy on standard dashboards: GPU compute utilization remains high — often 75–90% — because the workers continue executing attention kernels on the next scheduled chunk or processing newly arrived short prompts, but this compute is speculative in the sense that its outputs cannot be consumed by decode workers until the transfer backlog clears, meaning the prefill worker is building KV debt faster than it can be serviced. The metric an operator actually sees is MFU (Model FLOP Utilization) near nominal, token throughput per second looking strong on the prefill side, and GPU memory bandwidth utilization peaking — all green — while decode-side metrics tell a completely different story: decode worker idle time spikes, TTFT (time-to-first-token) for queued requests climbs, and inter-token latency on active decode sequences degrades because decode batches shrink as no new sequences can be admitted without their KV cache being present. This dashboard divergence is precisely what makes the failure mode insidious: the SRE watching GPU utilization sees no alarm, while the user-facing p95 TTFT is silently doubling. Nvidia's Dynamo serving framework documentation explicitly flags this as a "utilization-latency decoupling" pathology, noting that in disaggregated deployments aggregate GPU utilization can sit above 80% during periods when end-to-end request latency SLOs are being violated, because utilization measures work done, not useful work delivered. The deeper implication is that standard autoscaling policies keyed on GPU utilization will fail to trigger additional prefill capacity precisely when it is most needed — the system looks fully loaded, so the autoscaler either holds capacity constant or, if it's a shared-pool system, may even reduce prefill allocation to rebalance toward the apparently underutilized decode fleet, which is the opposite of the correct intervention.

During transfer bus saturation, prefill-side HBM fills with sealed-but-untransferred KV blocks that cannot be evicted because they are logically owned by in-flight requests whose decode workers are waiting for them — in vLLM's block allocator these blocks are reference-counted and pinned, so they are invisible to the eviction policy regardless of how long they have been sitting idle. As the backlog grows, the allocatable free-block pool shrinks, and the prefill worker's scheduler faces a hard constraint: it cannot begin chunked prefill for a new request if it cannot guarantee enough free blocks to hold that request's full KV output, because partial KV materialization mid-request with no place to write is not a degraded state — it is a deadlock, since the worker cannot roll back attention computation and the block it needs is held by a request that is itself waiting for the transfer bus to clear. This is the correctness boundary: the system transitions from "high latency" to "livelock" when the set of pinned untransferred blocks plus the blocks needed by the currently executing chunk exceeds total HBM block capacity, a condition that PagedAttention's original design (Kwon et al., 2023) did not need to handle because it assumed co-located prefill and decode sharing the same block pool with immediate KV availability. DistServe and subsequent disaggregated systems address this with a transfer credit mechanism — prefill workers request an allocation grant from the decode worker's memory manager before beginning prefill, so blocks are reserved on both ends before compute starts — but under bursty arrivals the credit round-trip (typically 1–3ms over RDMA) introduces its own queuing, and if credits are over-provisioned to hide that latency the decode worker's HBM becomes the pressure point instead, just shifting the correctness risk from prefill to decode. The practical threshold observed in Sarathi-Serve's ablations is that once in-flight pinned blocks exceed roughly 60–65% of prefill HBM block capacity, admission must be halted entirely or the system enters a regime where chunk scheduling decisions can no longer be made without risking the livelock condition — meaning the effective serving capacity of the prefill worker is substantially below what raw FLOP counts or memory bandwidth numbers would suggest.

The credit round-trip latency — typically 1–3ms over RDMA in systems like DistServe, but measurably higher (3–7ms) over commodity RoCE v2 with congestion control active — interacts with chunked scheduling epochs in a precise and painful way: if the scheduler runs epochs at fixed intervals (e.g., every 10ms in Sarathi-Serve's default configuration), a request that arrives just after an epoch boundary must wait up to one full epoch before its credit request is even issued, then another epoch before the credit response is incorporated into scheduling decisions, meaning the minimum TTFT floor from scheduling and credit overhead alone is 2×epoch_duration + RTT_credit, which at default settings is approximately 21–23ms before a single attention FLOP has been executed. This floor is not visible in microbenchmarks that measure prefill compute in isolation, which is why published TTFT numbers for disaggregated systems often look competitive with co-located serving at low load but diverge sharply when measured end-to-end with realistic request arrival timing rather than synchronized batch submission. The deeper issue is that credit latency and epoch duration are coupled constraints: reducing epoch duration to lower the scheduling wait increases scheduler invocation frequency and CPU overhead on the prefill coordinator, which at scale (hundreds of concurrent requests) can itself become a bottleneck, as observed in Mooncake (a disaggregated serving system deployed at Kimi) where the coordinator's scheduling loop became CPU-bound above roughly 400 concurrent prefill slots with 5ms epochs. An idle system does not escape this floor — in fact idle conditions can be worse in implementations that use adaptive epoch sizing, because a lightly loaded scheduler may extend epochs to reduce overhead, inadvertently increasing the minimum TTFT for the occasional arriving request precisely when there is ample capacity to serve it instantly. The implication for SLO design is significant: disaggregated serving has a structural TTFT floor that is architecture-determined rather than load-determined, meaning latency commitments for short, low-compute prompts (which could in principle be answered in 5–8ms with co-located serving) cannot be met by disaggregated systems without either very short epochs (expensive) or a fast-path bypass that routes short prompts outside the credit-and-chunk machinery entirely.

The canonical fast-path criterion in systems like Mooncake and internal Meta serving infrastructure is a token count threshold — typically 512 or 1024 tokens — below which a request bypasses the credit-and-chunk pipeline and is routed to a co-located prefill-decode worker that holds both KV memory and compute, eliminating transfer latency entirely; but this threshold must be applied after tokenization, because the only reliable length signal is the token count, not the character count or user-reported length, and tokenization for a 2000-character prompt with mixed languages, code, and markup can produce anywhere from 400 to 1800 tokens depending on vocabulary coverage. The classification correctness problem is therefore a pipeline ordering problem: in a high-throughput system, tokenization is itself batched and may run on CPU with 2–5ms latency for long inputs, meaning the admission decision that determines fast-path vs. slow-path routing cannot be made until after a delay that already consumes a significant fraction of the TTFT budget the fast path was designed to protect. Systems that attempt to predict token count from character count or byte length before tokenization — as some proxy-layer routers do — introduce misclassification at the tails of the distribution: a prompt that character-count heuristics predict as 400 tokens but actually tokenizes to 1100 tokens gets fast-pathed onto a co-located worker whose HBM was sized assuming short KV footprints, and if enough such misclassifications co-occur the co-located worker's block pool exhausts and it falls back to the same livelock risk described for the disaggregated path. Llama-based deployments with multilingual inputs face a particularly sharp version of this: fertility ratios for non-Latin scripts in SentencePiece and tiktoken vocabularies range from 1.5× to 4× relative to English, so a Thai or Arabic prompt that appears short in bytes can easily cross the fast-path threshold post-tokenization even when the pre-tokenization proxy confidently classified it as short. The deeper correctness concern is that fast-path misclassification is asymmetric in cost: a false negative (long prompt incorrectly fast-pathed) causes HBM pressure on the co-located worker, while a false positive (short prompt incorrectly slow-pathed) merely adds unnecessary credit-and-chunk overhead — so conservative threshold design intentionally accepts false positives, but this means a non-trivial fraction of genuinely short prompts still pay the disaggregated TTFT floor, defeating the purpose of the bypass for exactly the latency-sensitive requests it was meant to protect.

When block pool exhaustion occurs mid-prefill on a co-located worker, the runtime has four theoretical recovery options: (1) abort and requeue the request to the disaggregated slow path from token zero, (2) spill in-flight KV blocks to CPU DRAM or NVMe and continue prefill with a slower backing store, (3) evict KV blocks belonging to other requests currently in decode phase to free space, or (4) migrate the partially-completed KV state to a disaggregated prefill worker and resume from the last fully computed chunk boundary. Only options 3 and 4 preserve request correctness without full recomputation, and they have sharply different feasibility profiles: option 3 is immediately available but causes collateral latency damage to decode-phase requests that had no role in the misclassification, while option 4 requires the runtime to have implemented partial KV migration — transferring only the already-computed blocks to the receiving worker — which most production systems have not built because it was assumed unnecessary on the fast path. vLLM's current architecture does not support partial KV migration; its recovery path for mid-prefill OOM is request preemption with full recomputation, which for a 1024-token prompt that exhausted blocks at token 800 means discarding 800 tokens of attention computation and restarting, a correctness-preserving but efficiency-destroying outcome that also resets the TTFT clock entirely. The KV spill path (option 2) is implemented in some research systems — Infinite-LLM explored CPU offload for KV during prefill — but the bandwidth asymmetry between HBM and DRAM (typically 10–20× slower) means that once spill begins, the prefill worker's effective throughput collapses and the latency for the misclassified request becomes worse than if it had been slow-pathed from admission, while also consuming CPU memory bandwidth that may be needed by other system components. The fundamental difficulty with option 4, partial KV migration, is that chunk boundary alignment must be tracked at block granularity and the receiving disaggregated worker must be able to reconstruct the attention state from an arbitrary mid-sequence offset — which requires that the KV layout on the sending worker is identical to what the receiving worker expects, a constraint that breaks under heterogeneous hardware deployments where co-located and disaggregated workers may run different GPU generations with different optimal KV packing layouts.

Heterogeneous GPU generations within a single cluster — the increasingly common scenario where H100 prefill workers coexist with A100 decode workers, or where inference is spread across H100 SXM and H100 PCIe variants with different memory bandwidth profiles — break KV layout compatibility in two distinct ways: first, optimal tensor core alignment differs (H100 favors 16-byte aligned fp8 tiles while A100 operates on bf16 with different warp-level layout assumptions), and second, the KV head dimension packing that maximizes memory bandwidth on one architecture produces suboptimal or misaligned access patterns on the other, meaning a KV block written by an H100 prefill worker cannot be directly consumed by an A100 decode worker without a transcription step that reorders elements within each block. This transcription cost is not negligible: for a 128-head, 128-dimension-per-head KV layout at bf16, reformatting a 256-token block requires approximately 0.5–1ms of GPU time on the receiving worker, and if this happens at migration time rather than at write time it adds directly to TTFT; if it happens at decode time it adds to every decode step for the lifetime of the request, compounding the latency penalty across potentially hundreds of tokens. Quantized KV cache storage — INT8 or FP8 quantization applied to reduce HBM footprint, as implemented in TensorRT-LLM's KV cache quantization and explored in KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024) — interacts with layout compatibility in a particularly damaging way: the quantization scale factors are computed per-block or per-head on the prefill worker using statistics from the local attention distribution, and those scale factors are architecture- and precision-specific, meaning a receiving worker running a different quantization scheme cannot simply ingest the quantized blocks without either dequantizing and requantizing (expensive) or accepting numerical error from mismatched scale application (correctness risk). KVQuant's per-channel quantization scheme, which achieves strong quality preservation at 4-bit precision, is especially brittle here because the channel-wise scales are computed relative to the full sequence seen so far — migrating a partially-complete KV state means the scale factors on the sender reflect only tokens 0 through k, and the receiver must either reuse those scales (introducing error for tokens k+1 onward) or recompute them retroactively (requiring access to raw activations that were never stored). The practical implication is that heterogeneous disaggregated clusters must either mandate a canonical wire format for KV transfer — essentially a least-common-denominator layout in fp16 or bf16 with no quantization — that both sender and receiver transcode to and from locally, accepting the transcription overhead as a tax on migration, or they must restrict KV migration to homogeneous GPU pairs, which defeats much of the economic motivation for heterogeneous clusters where cheaper older GPUs handle decode and expensive newer GPUs handle compute-intensive prefill.
